papers.title: Exploring placebo response in Parkinson's disease clinical trials by comparing placebo arm progression on MDS-UPDRS to a natural history dataset.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: In Parkinson's disease (PD) clinical trials, measurement of disease progression may be influenced by placebo response. To explore this, we compared measurements of disease progression among clinical trial placebo arm participants to a natural history cohort by examining change in MDS-UPDRS scores over 24-months. METHODS: Data were sourced from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) natural history cohort and the placebo arms of clinical trials within the Critical Path for Parkinson's (CPP) database. Participants with confirmed PD within 2-years of diagnosis who were naïve to dopaminergic treatment were included. MDS-UPDRS scores over 24-months were compared by examining mean changes from baseline (CFB) and mean to standard deviation ratios (MSDR) of CFB. Mean CFBs and MSDRs were calculated for individual items at 12-months. RESULTS: In total, 430 and 183 participants from the PPMI and CPP databases were included, respectively. MDS-UPDRS Part 1 scores improved over the first 12-months for CPP participants (MSDR: -0.21), then reverted to baseline by 24-months (MSDR: 0.008). Participants in PPMI consistently declined over 24-months with MSDRs of 0.23 and 0.36 at 12- and 24-months, respectively. Aggregate level differences in progression on Part 2 and 3 were less apparent. CONCLUSIONS: A difference in progression on MDS-UPDRS Part 1 between placebo-enrolled clinical trial participants and registry participants potentially indicated placebo response. Clinical trial and natural history participants progressed similarly on the MDS-UPDRS total scores for Part 2 and 3. However, differences were noted at the item level, suggesting placebo response could have a differential effect on motor symptoms.

papers.title: Drug-resistant rest tremor is associated with slower disease progression in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Rest tremor in Parkinson's disease (PD) shows heterogeneous responsiveness to dopaminergic therapy. Drug-resistant rest tremor reflects mechanisms distinct from striatal dopamine depletion. We examined whether patients with drug-resistant rest tremor had a unique disease progression pattern. Using data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative, we studied 229 PD patients with rest tremor and 268 without rest tremor. Patients with rest tremor were classified by estimated drug responsiveness after adjustment for confounders. Linear mixed-effects models were used to compare longitudinal progression between groups, and mediation analyses to explore whether differences in disease progression were attributed to striatal DAT availability. PD patients with drug-resistant rest tremor exhibited milder motor and non-motor symptoms at baseline, and worsened more slowly in the MDS-UPDRS III non-tremor score than those with drug-responsive rest tremor (estimated difference in annual change: β = -1.54, p = 0.014) and those without rest tremor (β = -1.06, p = 0.016). These differences were not mediated by either baseline striatal DAT availability or its longitudinal changes.

papers.title: Rethinking single-pathology therapies by targeting inflammation and co-pathologies in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Co-expression of tau and amyloid-beta with α-syn pathology is shown in over 50% of Parkinson's Disease postmortem brains, and these patients present with enhanced cognitive decline and disease phenotype. This review integrates the known immune response in PD with co-pathology incidence, highlighting synergistic interactions between α-syn, tau and Aβ and how this promotes a distinct neuroinflammatory response leading to severe neuronal loss and cognitive symptoms. Based on this, we support the need for combinatorial therapeutic strategies to address this debilitating, yet common factor of disease.

papers.title: Motor and non-motor symptoms impact on different domains of capacity- and performance-related mobility measures in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Motor (MS) and non-motor symptoms (NMS) could contribute to mobility impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD), but the relative role of each remain unclear. While supervised mobility assessments capture capacity, wearable devices enable evaluation of real-world performance. In this cross-sectional study, 105 individuals with mild-to-moderate PD performed standardized tests of forward, backward walking and turning, and wore a consumer smartwatch for five consecutive days to record average daily steps. MS and NMS were evaluated using validated clinical scales. Robust multivariable regressions showed that MS and NMS explained a modest proportion of mobility variance, with stronger effects on capacity- than performance-related metrics. Tremor-dominant and postural instability/gait disorder subscore predicted supervised mobility, while akinetic-rigid subscore was associated with average daily steps. Executive dysfunction and fatigue emerged as the main NMS determinants of mobility. Overall, these findings suggest a complex interplay between MS and NMS and warrant the need for multidimensional mobility assessment in PD.

papers.title: Theta deep-brain stimulation improves cognitive performance in Parkinson's patients with cognitive impairments.
papers.abstract: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) can experience cognitive impairments linked to low frequency "theta" 4 Hz cortical activity and cognitive control. Our study investigated effects of 4 Hz subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) on cognitive performance in PD patients with cognitive impairments. We recruited 17 PD participants with (n = 10) and without (n = 7) cognitive impairment. We compared motor and cognitive performance during 4 Hz STN DBS, typical DBS for motor symptoms of PD (~130 Hz) and DBS OFF. Motor performance was tested by Part III of the Movement Disorders Society Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS-III). Cognitive performance was tested by the Multi-Source Interference Task (MSIT), which requires conflict resolution to respond accurately. Motor function improved with 4 Hz STN DBS and further improved with ~130 Hz STN DBS. Compared to DBS OFF, reaction times were decreased during 4 Hz STN DBS and were further decreased at ~130 Hz. Strikingly, 4 Hz DBS alone improved accuracy compared to DBS OFF and ~130 Hz STN DBS. These data suggest that 4 Hz STN stimulation can improve performance in PD patients with cognitive impairments. Our findings will guide therapies targeted at improving cognition in PD and could broaden low-frequency stimulation interventions.

papers.title: The Clinical Connectome in EBRAINS 2.0.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Neurological diseases, including stroke, Parkinson's disease (PD), and gliomas, have traditionally been interpreted through a focal-based lens, where symptoms are primarily attributed to the location and extent of neural damage. Converging evidence has reframed these conditions as circuitopathies, in which the disruption of brain networks underlies clinical manifestations. Yet, a network-integrated approach remains far from routine clinical practice. The aggregation of large datasets, which enables testing hypotheses about diagnosis, prognosis, or response to therapy across independent cohorts as well as prediction at the level of individual patients, is a critical step toward closing this translational gap. METHODS: We describe the Clinical Connectome initiative developed within Work Package 2 of the EBRAINS 2.0 project, a translational effort that aims to bridge network neuroscience and clinical neurology. We first review stroke, PD, and gliomas as complementary models of brain network disruption, highlighting how the different pathophysiological mechanisms converge on shared patterns of network perturbation. We then present the Platform for Human Imaging, a GDPR-compliant infrastructure that enables secure storage, harmonized processing, and controlled dissemination of multimodal neuroimaging and clinical data across European institutions. RESULTS: To date, the Clinical Connectome has aggregated data from over 7000 patients across institutions. A Delphi consensus panel, conducted in collaboration with the European Academy of Neurology (EAN), has established harmonized protocols for the prospective data acquisition in these disorders. CONCLUSIONS: By providing an integrated framework linking clinical neuroimaging to brain atlases and computational modeling, the Clinical Connectome aims to lay the foundations for network-based precision neurology.

papers.title: Levodopa-Entacapone-Carbidopa Intestinal Gel in advanced Parkinson's disease: clinical positioning, candidate profiling, and implementation roadmap.
papers.abstract: Device-aided therapies (DATs) for Parkinson's disease (PD) with motor complications encompass deep brain stimulation (DBS), intrajejunal and subcutaneous infusions. Levodopa-carbidopa-entacapone intestinal gel (LECIG) infusion is the most recent strategy to be included in the intrajejunal class. By adding peripheral catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibition, LECIG increases levodopa bioavailability, enabling a comparable dopaminergic effect at a reduced levodopa dose and infusion volume. Drawing on the discussion of a national advisory board of Italian movement disorder specialists, this perspective addresses the positioning of LECIG in PD patients with motor fluctuations. LECIG broadens the intrajejunal infusion landscape with a smaller device and potential metabolic advantages related to reduced 3-O-methyldopa generation. Two candidate scenarios predominate: the patient requiring a first infusional DAT after failure of optimized oral therapy who is ineligible for or declines DBS, and the patient already on a DAT with residual or worsening/re-emergent fluctuations. Favorable selection features include a levodopa-responsive, motor-fluctuation-predominant phenotype, documented COMT-inhibitor tolerance, absence of overt dementia with adequate caregiver support, a rationale for levodopa dose sparing (e.g., peripheral neuropathy risk), and concomitant dysphagia that features an additional niche benefitting of intestinal therapies. Cautionary or unfavorable features include levodopa-resistant axial disability, severe cognitive impairment, absence of caregiver support, COMT-inhibitor intolerance, and active neuropsychiatric symptoms, other than gastrointestinal contraindication for receiving gastrojejunostomy. Implementation barriers include the need for structured gastroenterology collaboration, and a potential cost-per-quality-adjusted-life-year higher than comparator DATs. papers.title: A GLUD2 variant aggravates Parkinson's disease pathology in A53T α-synuclein mice via the astrocyte-microglia C3‒C3aR pathway.
papers.journal: Cellular and molecular life sciences : CMLS
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss and α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation. The human-specific GLUD2 T1492G variant has been associated with an earlier onset of PD, but its pathogenic mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we generated A53T α-syn transgenic mice with astrocyte-specific expression of GLUD2 T1492G and investigated its effects on PD-related pathology. GLUD2 T1492G exacerbated α-syn pathology, nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurodegeneration, and motor impairment. Transcriptomic analysis identified complement-related inflammatory signaling as a major pathway altered by GLUD2 T1492G, whereas metabolomic profiling revealed disrupted metabolic homeostasis. Mechanistically, GLUD2 T1492G enhanced astrocytic C3 induction, promoted microglial C3aR/NF-κB-associated inflammatory activation, and amplified neuroinflammatory responses. Conditioned-medium transfer experiments, together with astrocyte-specific C3 knockdown and pharmacological inhibition of C3aR, supported the functional involvement of the astrocyte-microglia C3-C3aR signaling axis in GLUD2 T1492G-associated pathology. Collectively, our findings suggest that activation of the astrocyte-microglia C3-C3aR signaling axis contributes to GLUD2 T1492G-mediated exacerbation of PD pathology and highlight this pathway as a potential therapeutic target for PD.

papers.title: Investigation of disease-relevant lysine acetylation sites in α-synuclein enabled by non-canonical amino acid mutagenesis.
papers.abstract: Aggregates of α-synuclein (αS) are hallmarks of synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease (PD) and multiple system atrophy (MSA). We have recently shown that αS lysine acetylation in the soluble monomer pool varies between healthy controls, PD, and MSA patients. We used non-canonical amino acid mutagenesis to express and purify all 12 currently known disease-relevant variants of αS and studied their binding to membranes, as well as their aggregation propensities. We found that acetylation of lysine 12, 43, and 80 had particularly strong effects. To understand the implications for acetylation of monomeric αS found in healthy cells, we performed nuclear magnetic resonance experiments to study protein conformation and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy experiments to quantify lipid binding. We also investigated the effects of acetylation at lysine 12, 43, and 80 on fibril seeding in neurons. papers.title: Spatiotemporal organization of chaperone cocondensation drives stepwise disassembly of α-synuclein amyloid fibrils.
papers.abstract: α-Synuclein (α-syn) fibrils, a pathogenic hallmark of Parkinson's disease, are pathological aggregates associated with neurodegeneration. The human Hsp70/Hsp40 machinery can disassemble α-syn fibrils, yet the mechanism underlying this cooperative activity remains unclear. Here, we show that disaggregation is driven by a spatiotemporally organized hierarchy of cocondensates formed by Hsp40 (DnaJB1) and Hsp70 (Hsc70) on the fibril surface. Bulk disaggregation assays, super-resolution mapping and single-fibril optical trapping reveal that DnaJB1 nucleates condensates that template discrete Hsc70-enriched hotspots where ATP-dependent mechanical rupture occurs. As fragmentation proceeds, these condensates mature and merge into larger liquid-like droplets that engulf and dissolve fibril fragments, visualized by time-lapse microscopy and cryo-electron tomography. Moreover, modulating the condensation propensity of DnaJB1 by mutations markedly influences the disaggregation process; reduced phase separation is accompanied by diminished cocondensation and fibril clearance, whereas enhanced phase separation correlates with more efficient disassembly. Together, these findings support a model in which hierarchical, spatiotemporal condensation contributes to amyloid disassembly and suggest that targeting chaperone condensation may represent a strategy to enhance α-syn fibril clearance in Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: RNA G-quadruplexes in neurodegenerative disease: from structural regulation to proteinopathy.
papers.abstract: RNA G-quadruplexes (rG4) are dynamic RNA structures whose cellular abundance and folded state are regulated by a multitude of factors. rG4-binding proteins (rG4BPs) comprise a diverse group, including intrinsically disordered proteins such as FUS, TDP-43, and α-Synuclein, which are associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Moreover, rG4 are elevated in human tissue or disease models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Alzheimer's disease (AD), highlighting the importance of understanding the interplay between rG4 and rG4BPs. In this review, we examine the cellular mechanisms that regulate rG4 folding dynamics, with a particular focus on rG4BPs and cellular state. We outline the rG4BPs involved in ALS and PD, emphasizing their mechanisms of rG4 recognition. We discuss the current literature on the contributions of rG4s and rG4BPs to ALS, PD, AD, and Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) and their context-dependent effects on disease-associated protein phase transitions and aggregation. Finally, we highlight two emerging classes of molecules with therapeutic potential in neurodegenerative disease: rG4-containing and rG4-targeting. Together, this review explores the complex and context-dependent roles of rG4s in neurodegeneration and their potential as targets for manipulating RNA and protein biology.

papers.title: Inflammasomes: central mediators of neuroinflammatory neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: As life expectancy increases worldwide, the proportion of people aged 65 and older is expected to double by 2050 and these global demographic shifts will be accompanied by an increase in age-related neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). AD is the leading cause of dementia worldwide, characterized by progressive cognitive decline linked to amyloid beta accumulation, tau pathology, neuronal cell death and chronic neuroinflammation. PD is the most common movement disorder worldwide, characterized by progressive motor decline linked to alpha-synuclein accumulation, formation of Lewy bodies and neurites, dopaminergic neuron death, as well as chronic neuroinflammation. Increasing evidence implicates inflammasomes, intracellular multiprotein complexes that orchestrate innate immune responses, as key drivers of the neuroinflammatory milieu in AD and PD. The NLRP3 inflammasome, mostly expressed by microglia, has been shown to activate caspase-1, resulting in the cleavage and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 and promoting pyroptotic cell death within the central nervous system. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the molecular mechanisms of inflammasome activation, their pathological involvement in AD and PD, and the genetic underpinnings supporting their role. It further highlights emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at modulating inflammasome activity, evaluating preclinical outcomes and clinical trial progress. Understanding inflammasome dynamics provides critical insight into AD and PD pathophysiology and presents promising targets for future disease-modifying treatments.

papers.title: Selective Gut-Related Biomarker Profiles Define Parkinson Disease Trait and State.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Gut-brain-axis abnormalities are increasingly implicated in Parkinson disease (PD), but most studies examine individual biological compartments of this axis. We asked whether readily accessible stool and plasma-based biomarker profiles show broad or selective gut abnormalities in PD and whether the profiles associated with PD diagnosis (Trait) are the same as those associated with clinical severity (State). METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 211 participants with PD and 204 healthy controls. Twenty-four stool and plasma biomarkers were organized into an overall profile, three parent domains (microbiome/dysbiosis, gut barrier/inflammation, systemic inflammation/immune activation), and eight more focused mechanistic profiles. Rank-based Global Statistical Tests (GSTs) compared PD Trait and State. RESULTS: The overall profile showed no evidence of a PD vs. control difference (GST P=0.607; permutation P=0.521), whereas the domain of microbiome/dysbiosis differed (GST P=0.017; permutation P=0.013). Four of eight focused profiles differed nominally: microbial functional-groups, microbial functional-ratios, epithelial injury/bacterial translocation, and myeloid activation. Across PD clinical severity, overall-profile results differed (GST P=0.053; permutation P=0.037); both categories of microbiome/dysbiosis (GST P=0.023; permutation P=0.016) and microbial alpha-diversity (GST P=0.027; permutation P=0.031) differed. INTERPRETATION: The analyses detected differences associated with PD Trait and State in selected gut-related profiles rather than a detectable overall PD-control difference. Microbiome-related profiles showed the most consistent domain findings across PD Trait and State, but they are sufficiently different to suggest that causation and progression of PD follow distinctly different gut processes. These findings refine the concept of the "Parkinson gut" and prioritize the microbiome for mechanistic and interventional studies.

papers.title: Multimodal Imaging and Molecular Biomarkers of Co-Pathology Across the Parkinson's Disease-Dementia with Lewy Bodies Continuum.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) are increasingly viewed as regions of a single α-synuclein continuum rather than separate entities. Neuropathology shows that Lewy pathology rarely occurs alone: Alzheimer-type amyloid-β and tau, transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 kDa (TDP-43) inclusions, and cerebrovascular lesions accompany it as the rule rather than the exception, and this co-pathology contributes to the clinical heterogeneity observed across the continuum without mapping onto its clinical divisions. The open problem is no longer whether co-pathology matters but how to measure it in living patients and integrate that information for individualized care. This review is organized by proteinopathy (α-synuclein as the primary lesion, then amyloid-β, tau, and TDP-43/vascular co-pathology) and, within each, follows the modalities that interrogate it: molecular imaging, fluid and tissue biomarkers, and their downstream structural, metabolic, functional, and electrophysiological correlates. No single technique captures the co-pathological landscape. Profiling an individual's proteinopathy burden in vivo requires a deliberate combination of methods, and precision management of the PD-DLB continuum depends on this multimodal integration.

papers.title: Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing reveals DNA methylation and regulatory variant landscapes in de novo Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder whose molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Although DNA methylation has been implicated in PD pathogenesis, its genome-wide landscape and genetic regulation have not been comprehensively characterised. METHODS: We integrated whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 232 patients with de novo PD and 242 matched controls. DNA methylation levels were quantified at 26,280,503 CpG loci, followed by genome-wide mapping of methylation quantitative trait loci (mQTLs). Colocalisation and summary data-based Mendelian randomisation analyses were performed to identify methylation signals involved in PD risk. FINDINGS: We identified 47,586 differentially methylated positions corresponding to 5654 genes enriched in pathways relevant to PD, such as glutamatergic, cholinergic, and dopaminergic synaptic signalling. Genome-wide mQTL analysis revealed extensive genetic regulation of DNA methylation, yielding more than 512 million significant cis-mQTL associations. Integrative analyses further identified loci in which genetic susceptibility to PD may be mediated through DNA methylation and highlighted candidate genes, including SNCA, SLC45A3, NUCKS1, and SLC41A1. INTERPRETATION: Our findings suggest that genetic risk variants may influence PD susceptibility through DNA methylation-mediated regulatory mechanisms. These results expand current understanding of the molecular architecture of PD and provide a resource for prioritising epigenetic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. FUNDING: This study was supported by the Science and Technology Major Project of Hunan Provincial Science and Technology Department (2021SK1010), the Scientific Research Program of FuRong Laboratory (2023SK2099), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (82371274, 82571434), and the Natural Science Foundations of Hunan Province (2024JJ6679, 2024JJ42098).

papers.title: Modulation of genetic- and toxicant-induced Parkinson's disease outcomes by SV2C in C. elegans.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: Several proteins involved in dopaminergic neurotransmission have been implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), including synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2C (SV2C). At least seven SNPs in SV2C are associated with PD, including variants that modify: PD risk, PD risk in GBA carriers, PD severity, contribution of environmental factors (e.g., nicotine) to PD, and PD patient response to L-DOPA and dopamine therapies. Although the specific function of SV2C remains unknown, there is significant evidence supporting a role of SV2C in mediating vesicular dopamine content, vesicular trafficking, and neurotransmitter release. Furthermore, SV2C directly associates with α-synuclein and mediates the content of neurotoxicants within synaptic vesicles. Taken together, these data suggest that SV2C plays a critical role in mediating PD risk and pathogenesis. To investigate whether SV2C mediates PD outcomes, transgenic Caenorhabditis elegans

papers.title: Interleukin-1β as initiator of Alzheimer's disease neuropathogenesis: The Cytokine Hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation is the brain's innate immune system's response to many, if not all, neuronal stresses. Such neuronal stresses are associated with acute phase responses that include elevation of the synthesis of the neuronal membrane-spanning protein amyloid-β protein precursor (AβPP) and release of its secreted fragments (sAβPPα). In addition to other neuron sparing actions, neuronal stress and release of sAβPPα activate microglia located in cortical layers that are subject to development of the neuropathological changes of Alzheimer's disease viz extra-neuronal amyloid-β plaques and neurofibrillary tangle-laden neurons. Such microglia become enlarged and increase their expression of the pluripotent immune cytokine interleukin-1β (IL-1β). IL-1β is of particular interest as it is necessary for induction of the precursors of each of these neuropathological features that are necessary for both development of Alzheimer's disease and its neuropathological diagnosis. The role of IL-1β in development of these features includes: i) induction of amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques, via IL-1β induction of synthesis, translation, and processing of AβPP; and ii) of the neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer's disease and Lewy bodies of Parkinson's disease via IL-1β-induced increases in synthesis and activation of MAPK-p38, necessary for hyperphosphorylation of tau and α-synuclein. These actions offer evidence for a self-promoting cycle of IL-1β elevation, in response to neuronal insults as the driving force in a self-regenerating cycle of neuronal stress → microglial activation→ release of IL-1β → more Aβ plaques and neurofibrillary tangle bearing neurons, the two necessary neuropathological features diagnostic of Alzheimer's disease and thus The Cytokine Hypothesis.

papers.title: Downregulation of glycolysis-related transcripts is a shared feature between advanced age and early synucleinopathy.
papers.abstract: Aging, the primary risk factor for developing Parkinson's disease (PD), is associated with global decreases in glucose utilization. Nigrostriatal dopamine neurons have a high energy requirement; therefore, metabolic impairments are predicted to play a role in their susceptibility to degeneration. To understand the impact of advanced age on synucleinopathy, we examined glycolysis-related transcripts in young (2 mo) and aged (18 mo) male Fischer 344 rats. Evaluations were conducted during the peak of inclusion formation in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), two months following bilateral intrastriatal injections of either alpha-synuclein preformed fibrils (α-syn PFFs) or monomer. Advanced age did not impact the number of pSyn (α-syn phosphorylated at serine 129) inclusion-containing nigral neurons or loss of tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactive (THir) neurons. However, aged rats displayed significantly more compact pSyn inclusions in the SNc, indicative of advanced maturity. In both rats of advanced age and rats with pSyn inclusions, multiple glycolysis-related transcripts were decreased, including Gpi, Pfkm, Aldoa, Tpi1, Pgk1, Pgam1, Eno2 and Pkm. Only Hk2 displayed a trend toward increased expression in both the aged and pSyn-bearing SNc and was observed to be significantly increased in aged rats with pSyn inclusions. Hexokinase 2 (HK2) protein was primarily expressed in microglia but also expressed in pSyn-bearing SNc neurons. These findings suggest that co-occurrent glycolytic deficits associated with aging and pSyn inclusion formation result in metabolically compromised SNc neurons that may attempt to regulate glycolysis via increased HK2 expression.

papers.title: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy-Type Co-Pathology in Synucleinopathies.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: While Lewy bodies may occur in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), PSP neuropathological change (PSP-NC) is seldom investigated as co-pathology in Parkinson's disease (PD) with Lewy body pathology or multiple system atrophy (MSA), leaving its clinicopathological significance unclear. OBJECTIVES: To determine the frequency, distribution, clinical, and neuroimaging correlates of PSP-NC in 23 PD and 19 MSA cases. RESULTS: Six PD cases (26.1%) showed PSP-NC, including two (8.6%) fulfilling Rainwater criteria and four with early-stage pathology; one PD case showed nigral tau astrogliopathy (NITAG). One MSA case (5.2%) met PSP-NC criteria, and two (10.5%) showed NITAG. PSP-NC/NITAG cases tended to be older, with modest clinical effect, mainly falls, and heterogeneous magnetic resonance imaging findings with some cases showing features of PSP. CONCLUSIONS: PSP-NC is likely a late-emerging co-pathology in PD and, less often, in MSA, with subtle clinical impact. These findings inform interpretation of biomarkers and α-synuclein-targeted therapeutic trials. © 2026 The Author(s). Movement Disorders published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Intranasal apelin-13 attenuates neuroinflammation and neuropathological alterations in an LPS-ınduced parkinson's disease model.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuron loss and neuroinflammation. This study evaluated the effects of apelin-13 on motor and olfactory dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and neuropathological alterations in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced PD-like rat model. Rats were assigned to the control (n = 8), LPS (n = 15), Apelin-N + LPS (intranasal) (n = 15), and Apelin-I + LPS (intraperitoneal) (n = 15) groups. LPS (100 µg/rat/day) was administered intranasally for 30 days. Apelin-13 was administered intranasally (100 ng/g/day) or intraperitoneally (20 nmol/kg/day), starting three days before LPS and continuing throughout LPS exposure. Behavioral tests were performed, followed by molecular, histopathological, and immunohistochemical analyses of the olfactory bulb, substantia nigra and striatum. LPS administration caused significant motor and olfactory impairments (p < 0.05), increased NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-18 (IL-18) mRNA expression and α-synuclein, ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (IBA-1), Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2), and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) immunopositivity (p < 0.001), and decreased tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) immunopositivity (p < 0.001) compared to the control group. Apelin-13 treatment significantly reversed these alterations (p < 0.05-0.001), with improvements observed following both intranasal and intraperitoneal administration. Histopathological findings revealed marked hyperemia, perineuronal edema, and neuronal damage following LPS administration, which were markedly attenuated by apelin-13 treatment. These findings support further investigation of the apelin/APJ system as a potential neuroprotective target in PD.

papers.title: Methionine restriction and its underlying molecular mechanisms in brain health and diseases.
papers.abstract: Sulfur-containing amino acids, particularly methionine, play a central role in brain metabolism and the maintenance of neural homeostasis. Perturbations in brain methionine metabolism have been associated with a wide spectrum of behavioral and neuropsychiatric outcomes, including anxiety- and depression-like phenotypes, as well as cognitive and behavioral impairments relevant to schizophrenia, fear processing, and bipolar disorder. In addition, brain methionine metabolism intersects with multiple molecular pathways implicated in major neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, and Parkinson's disease. Accumulating evidence over the past two decades indicates that methionine intake and the integrity of the methionine metabolic network constitute a critical regulatory axis in brain health, capable of exerting both neuroprotective and neurotoxic effects in a context-dependent manner. Moderate dietary methionine restriction induces adaptive metabolic reprogramming in the brain, enhancing learning, memory, adult neurogenesis, and synaptic resilience, while simultaneously strengthening antioxidant defenses and resistance to oxidative stress. In contrast, excessive methionine intake disrupts neuronal homeostasis, promotes microglial activation, and amplifies neuroinflammatory signaling, thereby compromising neural integrity. Notably, these effects exhibit pronounced sex specificity, highlighting the modulatory roles of hormonal and genetic factors in methionine metabolism. Elucidating this duality may enable the development of precision-based dietary and metabolic interventions targeting methionine-related pathways for the prevention and treatment of psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. This review summarizes current research on dietary methionine restriction and its effects on neurological function, psychiatric conditions, and neurodegenerative diseases, with a particular focus on the underlying molecular mechanisms.

papers.title: The Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis in Neurological and Neuropsychiatric Disorders: A Literature Review.
papers.abstract: The gut-brain axis is a bidirectional communication network linking the GI tract and central nervous system via neural, immune, endocrine, and metabolic pathways. Growing evidence suggests that alterations in the gut microbiota are associated with the pathophysiology and clinical features of several neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), anxiety disorders, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). This narrative review used a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Wiley Online Library to identify relevant literature published from January 1, 2010, through the final search date of June 25, 2026. Proposed mechanisms linking gut dysbiosis with neurological dysfunction include alterations in intestinal and blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, systemic inflammatory signaling, microglial activation, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysregulation, changes in neurotransmitter pathways, and altered production of microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Advanced profiling technologies, including 16S rRNA sequencing, whole-genome metagenomics, and metabolomics, have significantly enhanced the identification of disease-associated microbial signatures. These observations have stimulated interest in microbiome-targeted interventions, including probiotics, prebiotics, psychobiotics, synbiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), live biotherapeutic products, and dietary modification; however, evidence supporting their clinical efficacy in neurological disorders remains limited and heterogeneous. Across the disorders reviewed, recurrent findings include alterations in microbial composition, intestinal barrier function, inflammatory signaling, and microbial metabolites. However, specific taxonomic signatures vary considerably among studies. Human evidence remains predominantly associative, while stronger

papers.title: Long-Term Health-Related Quality of Life After Globus Pallidus Internus Deep Brain Stimulation Versus Optimized Medical Therapy in Advanced Parkinson Disease: A Prospective Nonrandomized Cohort Study.
papers.journal: Neuromodulation : journal of the International Neuromodulation Society
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the globus pallidus internus (GPi) is a well-established therapeutic intervention for advanced Parkinson disease (PD). Nonetheless, real-world data regarding the long-term effects of GPi-DBS on health-related quality of life (HRQoL), as compared with optimized medical therapy (MED), are limited. This study sought to compare five-year HRQoL outcomes between GPi-DBS and MED in patients with advanced PD and to identify independent predictors of sustained long-term improvements in HRQoL. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this single-center, prospective, nonrandomized cohort study, a total of 365 patients with advanced PD underwent screening, and 216 were enrolled after multidisciplinary evaluation to receive GPi-DBS (n = 119) or continued MED (n = 97). At the five-year follow-up, 87 patients in the GPi-DBS group and 61 in the MED group completed the assessments. Propensity-score matching (PSM) at a 1:1 ratio balanced baseline demographic characteristics and disease phenotype, resulting in comparable cohorts (GPi-DBS, n = 32; MED, n = 32). The primary outcome was the summary index of the 39-item PD Questionnaire (PDQ-39). Secondary outcomes included the score on part III of the Unified PD Rating Scale (UPDRS-III), the Barthel Index for activities of daily living (ADL), the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, and the levodopa equivalent daily dose. Longitudinal changes in HRQoL were evaluated with the use of mixed-effects models, and multivariable linear regression was used to identify predictors of five-year improvement in the PDQ-39 summary index. RESULTS: Patients receiving GPi-DBS exhibited significant reductions in PDQ-39 scores at both one year (mean change, -13.0; p < 0.001) and five years (mean change, -10.6; p < 0.001). papers.title: Revisiting Stimulation Polarity in Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation: Monopolar Anodic Programming for Freezing of Gait and Tremor Refractory to Cathodic Stimulation-A Case Series and Focused Clinical and Mechanistic Review.
papers.journal: Neuromodulation : journal of the International Neuromodulation Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tremor and freezing of gait (FOG) are two disabling symptoms that may defy available medical or stimulation therapies in some patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of anodic stimulation in treatment-resistant FOG and tremors in patients with PD receiving subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Five patients with PD, four with treatment-refractory FOG and one with recurrent tremor, after bilateral STN DBS, were systematically assessed under both cathodic and anodic stimulation, with all other stimulation parameters held constant to isolate polarity-dependent effects. RESULTS: Compared with conventional cathodic stimulation, anodic stimulation was associated with clinically meaningful improvement in FOG and tremor in this selected cohort. CONCLUSION: Anodic stimulation may offer an alternative programming strategy for resistant FOG and tremor cases. The findings need to be further confirmed by mechanistic and longitudinal studies integrating imaging, neurophysiology, and computational modeling to optimize individualized therapy.

papers.title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability.
papers.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Clear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. METHODS: We used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinson's disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. RESULTS: Combined saccade-vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade-assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7-49.3%; p≈0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. SIGNIFICANCE: Binocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

papers.title: Pre-Post Changes in Balance-Related Outcomes Following Session-by-Session Patient-Specific Dynamic Cycling in People With Parkinson's Disease: A Preliminary Study.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cycling-based aerobic exercise has demonstrated benefits for motor symptoms and gait in individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD). However, whether adaptive dynamic cycling interventions improve balance-related outcomes remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate changes in balance confidence, clinical balance, functional mobility, and instrumented Timed Up and Go (iTUG) outcomes following session-by-session patient-specific dynamic cycling (SSPSDC) intervention in people with PD. METHODS: Twenty-eight individuals with PD participated in a 4-week cycling program consisting of twelve exercise sessions. Balance confidence was assessed using the Activities-specific Balance Confidence (ABC) scale, clinical balance using the Berg Balance Scale (BBS) and Mini-BESTest, and functional mobility using the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test. In a subset of participants, inertial sensors were used during TUG test to obtain instrumented mobility metrics, including turning and transitional parameters. Pre-post differences were analyzed using paired-samples t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate based on the distribution of paired differences, with effect sizes reported as Cohen's d or r, respectively. RESULTS: No significant changes were observed in ABC (n = 23), BBS or Mini-BESTest (n = 16), TUG (n = 19), or iTUG metrics (n = 11) (all p > 0.05). Effect sizes across outcomes were generally trivial to small. CONCLUSION: A short 4-week SSPSDC program was not associated with significant pre-post changes in balance-related outcomes in individuals with PD. While cycling may support motor function and cardiovascular fitness, additional balance- or gait-specific training may be necessary to improve balance-related function. Additional experiments with dynamic cycling are necessary to further investigate its role in improving balance or gait-specific measures.

papers.title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation of the Laryngeal and Cerebellar Motor Cortex Combined With Speech and Voice Therapy in People With Parkinson's Disease: A Preliminary Study.
papers.journal: Journal of voice : official journal of the Voice Foundation
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate the effects of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on the laryngeal motor cortex (LMC) and cerebellar transcranial direct current stimulation (ctDCS) associated with speech and voice therapy in hypokinetic dysarthria (HD) in people with Parkinson's disease (PD). METHODS: A preliminary intervention study was conducted with 16 participants over 10 consecutive days, with a 48-hour interval corresponding to the weekend. Participants were divided into two groups according to the intervention period: one group underwent anodal ctDCS (n = 8), and the other anodal tDCS on the LMC (n = 8). Concurrent with stimulation of these sites, speech and voice therapy was provided, consisting of the straw phonation in water technique followed by exercises from the speech therapy booklet, which included articulatory and prosodic training. RESULTS: In both groups (tDCS in LMC and ctDCS), there was an improvement postintervention in the phonation subsystem (P = 0.037 and P = 0.008, respectively). However, regarding the other components, the results varied according to the site stimulated: the LMC group showed improvements in articulation (P = 0.020), whereas the ctDCS group showed improvement in respiration (P = 0.037). Concerning the resonance and prosody, no significant differences were observed between the preintervention and postintervention periods. CONCLUSIONS: Both stimulation sites were associated with improvements in phonation, which may be partly attributable to the speech and voice therapy provided equally to both groups. However, differences were also observed according to the targeted neurostimulation site: stimulation in the LMC showed benefits inherent to the speech articulation subsystem, and ctDCS for the breathing subsystem. The choice of stimulation target thus proved to be an important aspect to consider during the rehabilitation of HD in PD.

papers.title: Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation for Dysarthria in Parkinson's Disease: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Dysarthria is one of the common symptoms among patients with Parkinson's disease. It is mainly characterized by reduced volume, monotonous pitch, weakened stress, unstable speech rate, inaccurate pronunciation, and impaired rhythm, severely affecting the patients' quality of life and mental health. Numerous studies have indicated that the efficacy of pharmacotherapy and surgical therapy on articulation function remains inconsistent and controversial. In recent years, relevant studies have revealed that non-invasive brain stimulation can improve phonation in patients with Parkinson's disease, regulate the excitability of the stimulated brain regions and the functional connectivity between these regions and the cortices associated with speech control. However, existing research on non-invasive brain stimulation for the treatment of dysarthria in Parkinson's disease remains limited, characterized by inconsistent stimulation parameters, small sample sizes, and insufficient investigation into the underlying mechanisms. This narrative review summarizes the common techniques in non-invasive brain stimulation, including the research progress, potential mechanisms, and safety of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and transcranial direct current stimulation in the treatment of speech disorders in patients with Parkinson's disease. The aim is to further explore the feasibility of non-invasive brain stimulation in the treatment of dysarthria in Parkinson's disease, providing references and future directions for clinical practice.

papers.title: Silent Regulators, Loud Impact: The Role of Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in the Regulation of Parkinson's Disease and Related Genes.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by a spectrum of neurological and non-neurological symptoms. How, when, or why the disease starts is still largely unknown. The predominant pathology has been motor symptoms arising from the death of dopaminergic neurons with α-synuclein protein aggregation; however, several alternative hypotheses have emerged that lead to differential disease onset. Although age, genetic, and environmental factors have been shown to be the leading causes of PD, growing evidence suggests that the non-coding regions of the human genome contribute more to disease pathology than previously known. One particular type of non-coding element, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), has emerged as an important regulator of PD pathogenesis by modulating key genes and disease-relevant pathways. Recent studies highlight the involvement of lncRNAs in regulating PD-associated genes, including LRRK2, SNCA, PINK1/PRKN, and in cellular processes such as neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, autophagy, and α-synuclein aggregation. Several lncRNAs, including HOTAIR, MALAT1, and NEAT1, are differentially expressed in PD models and patient tissues, where they influence neuronal survival and stress responses through mechanisms such as microRNA (miRNAs) sponging, chromatin modification, and paraspeckle formation. In this review, we critically evaluate the epigenetic, transcriptional, post-transcriptional, translational, and post-translational mechanisms through which lncRNAs regulate PD-associated pathways, either directly or via miRNAs. Furthermore, we have systematically evaluated individual lncRNAs implicated in in vitro and in vivo PD models, with an emphasis on the competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) activity of lncRNAs, their downstream molecular targets, and their contribution to dopaminergic neuron vulnerability.
